Whose Jobs? Men, Women and the China Shock

Model report 2 — Diversity in a Globalized World

Author

Popescu (example report)

Published

September 9, 2026

Show Code 
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

zones <- st_read("data/china_shock/china_shock_gender.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)
jobs  <- read.csv("data/china_shock/china_shock_gender_long.csv")

The question

When economists talk about the China shock, they usually talk about towns. A town had factories, the factories closed, the town suffered. Autor, Dorn and Hanson measured this carefully, and their finding is now famous: the American places most exposed to Chinese imports lost the most factory jobs.

But a town is not a single person, and a factory is not a single kind of job. Some American factories made clothes and shoes, and those factories employed a great many women. Others made car parts and machinery, and those employed mostly men.

If Chinese competition arrived in one kind of factory before the other, then the same shock would have reached different people at different moments. That is what we set out to look for.

Our question is simple: when Chinese imports arrived, did men and women lose factory work in the same way?

Why we thought the answer might be no

China did not begin by exporting everything at once. It began with what was cheapest to make: clothing, shoes, fabric, simple household goods. Those were exactly the American industries that employed women in large numbers.

The picture changed around 2001, when China joined the World Trade Organization and its exports widened into furniture, metal products and electronics assembly — industries where the American workforce was more male.

So there is a reason to expect the shock to have had a sequence. First the industries where women worked, then the industries where men worked. Whether that is really what happened is something the data can tell us.

What we are working with

The country is divided into 722 commuting zones. A commuting zone is simply a local job market: a cluster of towns close enough together that people live in one and work in another. It is a better unit than a city, because it captures the area a person could realistically find work in without moving house.

For each zone we know how much Chinese import competition it faced, and how much factory employment changed — separately for women and for men. We have this for two stretches of time, 1990 to 2000 and 2000 to 2007.

Show Code 
head(jobs[, c("czone", "period", "sex", "exposure", "change", "base")], 4)
  czone    period   sex exposure    change     base
1   100 1990-2000 Women 5.293786 -3.885627 14.52270
2   100 1990-2000   Men 5.293786 -3.916344 26.79467
3   100 2000-2007 Women 6.619861 -4.141328 10.63707
4   100 2000-2007   Men 6.619861 -5.032735 22.87832

Each row is one zone, in one period, for one sex. The column base records how much of that zone’s employment the group held in factories at the start.

That last column deserves a moment, because it turns out to matter more than anything else in this report. At the beginning of the period, women held around 7% of local employment in factory work. Men held around 15% — roughly twice as much. Men were simply more likely to work in a factory to begin with.

This means we have to be careful later on. Losing three points of employment when you started with seven is a very different experience from losing three points when you started with fifteen, even though the number is the same. We will come back to this once we have seen the first results.

One small note on the data. We left out a handful of zones where almost nobody worked in factories at the start. In those places, dividing by the starting number produces percentages that are technically enormous and practically meaningless.

Where the shock arrived

The clearest way to begin is geographically. Before asking what happened, we can ask where women worked in factories in the first place.

Show Code 
ggplot(zones) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = mfg_women_start), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "rocket", direction = -1,
                       name = "% of women\nin factories") +
  labs(title = "Where women worked in factories, 1990") +
  theme_void()

The dark band is unmistakable. It runs down through the Carolinas, into Georgia and across Tennessee — the American textile belt, where clothing and fabric were made.

Now the second question: where did Chinese imports actually land?

Show Code 
ggplot(zones) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = exposure), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1, trans = "sqrt",
                       name = "Import\ncompetition") +
  labs(title = "Where Chinese import competition was strongest, 1990–2000") +
  theme_void()

The two maps describe nearly the same country. The places facing the most Chinese competition in the 1990s were, to a considerable extent, the places where women worked in factories. That overlap is the first real evidence that the question we are asking is the right one.

And if the imports arrived where women worked, we would expect the job losses to appear there too.

Show Code 
ggplot(zones) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = mfg_change_women), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis",
                       name = "Change in\nwomen's factory\nemployment") +
  labs(title = "Change in women's factory employment, 1990–2000") +
  theme_void()

They do. Three maps, read in order, tell a coherent story: the imports came to the textile belt, and the textile belt is where women’s factory jobs went.

Comparing men and women directly

Maps show where things happened. To compare men and women we need to put them side by side.

In the graph below, every dot is one commuting zone. Moving right means the zone faced more Chinese competition. Moving down means it lost more factory employment. If import competition and job loss go together, the dots should slope downwards — and if the two groups were affected differently, the two lines should differ.

Show Code 
first <- jobs[jobs$period == "1990-2000", ]

ggplot(first, aes(x = exposure, y = change, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Women = "#b44527", Men = "#0f6f96"), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "In the 1990s, the line for women falls much faster",
       x = "Import competition from China",
       y = "Change in factory employment (percentage points)") +
  theme_minimal()

They differ, and not subtly. The red line for women drops steeply; the blue line for men is almost flat. Through the 1990s, more Chinese competition went together with a substantial fall in women’s factory employment and very little change in men’s.

The grey bands around each line show how confident we can be about where the line sits. They barely touch, which tells us this gap is unlikely to be an accident of which zones happened to be in the data.

So far the story holds up. The next question is whether it stayed true.

What happened after 2001

If the industry explanation is right, the pattern should change in the second period, once China moved into furniture and metals and electronics. So we draw the same graph again, with one panel for each stretch of time.

Show Code 
ggplot(jobs, aes(x = exposure, y = change, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Women = "#b44527", Men = "#0f6f96"), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ period) +
  labs(title = "Counting percentage points",
       subtitle = "The two lines start far apart and end up together",
       x = "Import competition from China",
       y = "Change in factory employment (percentage points)") +
  theme_minimal()

This looks like a clean confirmation. In the left panel the lines are far apart. In the right panel they lie almost on top of one another, with the blue line for men now falling as steeply as the red one. Read this way, the shock appears to have started as a women’s shock and then broadened to include men — exactly the sequence the industry story predicted.

It would be easy to stop here. We think that would be a mistake.

The same picture, measured differently

Remember that men began with roughly twice as much factory employment as women. Every number in the graph above is counted in percentage points of a zone’s total employment — and percentage points do not mean the same thing to a group that started at 7% as to a group that started at 15%.

Consider the second period. Women’s employment falls by about 0.36 points and men’s by about 0.43. In percentage points, men lose more. But 0.36 out of a starting 7 is a larger share of what women had than 0.43 out of a starting 15 is of what men had.

So there is a second, equally reasonable way to count: not how many points of the local job market disappeared, but how much of each group’s own factory work disappeared. Here is precisely the same data, measured that way.

Show Code 
ggplot(jobs, aes(x = exposure, y = rel_change, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Women = "#b44527", Men = "#0f6f96"), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ period) +
  labs(title = "Counting how much of each group's own factory work disappeared",
       subtitle = "Measured this way, the red line stays below the blue one throughout",
       x = "Import competition from China",
       y = "Change as a share of where each group started (%)") +
  theme_minimal()

The convergence is gone. Measured against what each group had to begin with, the red line sits below the blue line in the first period and in the second. Nothing hands over from women to men. Women simply lose a larger share of their factory work throughout.

Same zones, same years, same underlying numbers — and two different conclusions, depending on nothing more than which denominator we chose.

What we take from this

Three things seem solid to us.

The first is that the imports arrived where women worked. The maps line up too well for that to be coincidence: the textile belt was both the heart of women’s factory employment and the front line of Chinese competition.

The second is that in the 1990s women’s factory work fell considerably faster than men’s. Both ways of counting agree on this, and the gap in that first period is wide on either measure.

The third is the one we did not expect, and it is the reason this report exists. Whether that gap closed after 2001 depends entirely on how you choose to count. If you count points of the local job market, men catch up and the story becomes one of a shock that moved. If you count how much of each group’s own work vanished, women remain worse off and nothing moves at all.

We cannot say which of these is the right way to count, because they are not competing answers to one question — they are answers to two different questions. How much did this town’s job market change? is a question about places. How much of women’s factory work disappeared? is a question about people. Both are worth asking. What we would not accept is a report that quietly picks one and presents it as the whole finding.

The maps earn their place here too. The graphs can show that import competition and job loss move together, but only the maps show that they moved together in the textile belt specifically — and it was seeing that overlap that made us suspect the industries mattered at all.

What this report does not show

We have not shown that Chinese imports caused any of this. We have shown that places with more import competition also had larger falls in factory employment, which is not the same claim. Something else could have been driving both, and establishing cause would need methods we have not used here.

Our explanation about clothing first and furniture later is a plausible story that fits the timing and fits the maps, but we did not test it. Checking it properly would mean looking at which industries actually drove the import competition in each period. That data exists and we did not use it.

We have also been counting shares of employment rather than people. A falling share can mean that factory jobs disappeared, or that the rest of the local economy grew around them. And two periods, however suggestive, are two snapshots — they cannot tell us whether a change happened gradually or all at once.

How we used AI

What we did AI? What we asked How we checked
Fixing a blank map Yes Why nothing appeared when we drew it Compared with the class example, re-ran it
Choosing map colours Yes Which colour scale suits skewed numbers Tried three and chose by looking
Deciding the question No — —
Writing the interpretation No — —
The WTO date Yes When China joined the WTO Checked the WTO website: December 2001

The prompt that mattered most was this one:

“I have a table called jobs with one row per zone, per period, per sex. I want one scatterplot per period, with men and women in different colours. Show me the ggplot code and explain each line.”

Its first answer put both periods into a single panel, where everything overlapped and no pattern was visible. Adding facet_wrap(~ period) split them, and that is when we could see the two lines converging — which set up the whole second half of this report.

Where the data comes from

Autor, D. H., Dorn, D., & Hanson, G. H. (2013). The China Syndrome: Local Labor Market Effects of Import Competition in the United States. American Economic Review, 103(6), 2121–2168.
